description: Space4Future is tackling the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge at NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about space exploration, astrophysics, and data science. We are looking for enthusiastic teammates skilled in Python/data analysis, space science/astronomy, or UI/UX design & storytelling. We analyze cosmic data and build impactful space solutions together.
summary: SkyShift is a web app that lets anyone see what moved or changed in NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colors, but using its public data takes archive queries, FITS files, and photometry code, so moving and changing objects stay hidden in the archive. In SkyShift, you type a name or coordinates and watch real SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA as a time-lapse across surveys. The app measures the object's 102-color spectrum, scans the field for sources that moved or changed brightness, compares them with the Gaia DR3 and CatWISE catalogues, and explains its verdict with every check shown. An AI guide explains the results at the user's level and in their language. On the challenge's test objects, SkyShift measures WISE 0855 moving 7.7 arcseconds a year (published: 8.1) and finds the methane dip that marks Epsilon Indi B as a T-type brown dwarf. This matters because the Sun's coldest neighbors are found by exactly this mix of motion and infrared color, and SkyShift puts that search in everyone's hands.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SkyShift turns NASA's SPHEREx survey into something anyone can explore. You open the 3D Sky Navigator (9,096 real stars), pick one of the five challenge objects or type any coordinates, and SkyShift fetches the real SPHEREx images for that patch of sky from NASA/IPAC IRSA.

- Time-lapse: images from each six-month survey are combined and played in sequence, so you can watch an object move or change brightness. A sharper fine view and a smoother view are available.

- Spectrum: every SPHEREx image sees the object at a slightly different wavelength, so SkyShift builds a 102-color spectrum from 0.75 to 5 micrometers, with problem pixels flagged.

- Scan: SkyShift compares the first and last surveys, detects sources above 5 sigma, and measures shifts well below one pixel, counting a change only when it is larger than its error.

- Classify: a transparent reading of the measured colors, motion, and catalogues (for example, "a very cold object, likely a brown dwarf"), with each check shown, such as the methane dip at 3.3 micrometers.

- Layers: Gaia DR3 stars and CatWISE cold-object candidates (red infrared sources that Gaia does not see), quality flags, and reference images from WISE, 2MASS, and DSS2.

- Ask AI: a guide powered by Google Gemini that receives SkyShift's own measurements as context and explains them at a beginner, student, or expert level, in the user's language.

- Share: every view has its own link and embed code, and the time-lapse can be saved as a GIF or WebM video.

- Always current: the server checks IRS A daily for the next SPHEREx data release, so new six-month surveys appear without a code change.

- Hazard context: live official asteroid data from NASA/JPL (SBDB, Sentry, close approaches), clearly labelled as context, not a warning system.

- Discovery inbox: a practice area where people vote 'real,' 'artefact,' or 'unsure' on clearly labeled example candidates, showing how a community review would work.

VALIDATION ON REAL DATA

We tested SkyShift on the challenge objects with SPHEREx DR1 data:

- WISE 0855-0714: measured motion of 7.7 arcseconds a year to the west (published: about 8.1); classified as a very cold object, likely a brown dwarf.

- Epsilon Indi B: measured a motion of 4.2 to 5.4 arcseconds a year (published: about 4.7) and a clear methane dip that marks a T-type brown dwarf.

- Barnard's Star, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis are so bright that they saturate the detectors; SkyShift says so instead of reporting false numbers.

The code has 19 automated tests and 0 accessibility violations (axe-core).

BENEFITS

- For the public and students: real NASA data in a few clicks, with plain-language explanations and no software to install.

- For citizen scientists: motion and color on one screen, cross-matched with Gaia and CatWISE, so a candidate can be judged quickly.

- For educators: shareable links and videos of real objects moving across the sky.

- For astronomers: a fast first look at any field, with downloadable spectra (CSV) and every measurement explained.

INTENDED IMPACT

The Sun's coldest neighbors, brown dwarfs and free-floating planets, are too faint to see in visible light. They are found by their motion and their infrared colors. SkyShift puts that search in everyone's hands, helps more people use SPHEREx data, and lays the base for a community that vets candidates before experts follow them up.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.

- Front end: React 19, Vite, three.js (3D Sky Navigator), Aladin Lite (reference images); our own FITS reader with SIP astrometry, image stacking, and photometry.

- Back end: Python, Node.js 24 server on Google Cloud Run, Cloud Storage (short-lived image cache), Firestore (votes), Secret Manager, Gemini API.

- Data: SPHEREx DR1 (IRSA SIA cutouts), Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 (IRSA TAP), Yale Bright Star Catalogue (NASA HEASARC), NASA/JPL SBDB, Sentry and CAD APIs, WISE/2MASS/DSS2 HiPS.

- Testing: Vitest and axe-core.

- Hardware: a Windows 11 laptop; no special hardware is needed, and the app runs in any modern browser.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

SPHEREx was built to map colors, not motion. SkyShift uses its repeated six-month surveys as a motion survey and combines them with its 102 colors on the same screen. Earlier flipbook projects with WISE could show that something moved, using two colors. SkyShift also answers what it is. The AI guide is grounded in SkyShift's own measurements rather than guessing, and the app adapts to the person: their level, their language, and the object they are looking at.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Honesty about data: only real SPHEREx data; every verdict shows its checks; saturated stars are reported as such, and example content is labelled as an example.

- Ease of use: plain language, a three-step guide, keyboard access, and readable contrast, so non-astronomers can use it.

- Cost and sustainability: small image cutouts instead of full images, a cache that expires after 30 days, free-tier services, and a budget alert.

- Privacy and openness: no accounts or sign-in; preferences stay in the visitor's browser.

- Responsible AI: the guide is told not to invent values and to point to official sources (NASA JPL CNEOS, ESA) for impact risk.
